text:
Curriculum research supports comparing meaningful schedules against random and reversed schedules with identical pacing; these controls separate ordering from other scheduling effects ([Weinshall et al., 2018](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/weinshall18a/weinshall18a.pdf)). Benefits also depend on training budget, making a fixed horizon essential ([When Do Curricula Work?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.03107)). Random loss weighting can itself be competitive, so outperforming equal weights alone provides weak evidence for a particular curriculum ([Random Weighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.10603)).

Experimental recommendation: for L_t = Σ_k w_k(t)L_k, compare the schedule with constant weights w̄_k = (1/T)Σ_t w_k(t), matching cumulative coefficients for every loss. Keep loss reductions, normalization, initialization, optimizer state, learning-rate schedule, sampled minibatches, masking/negative samples, and update count identical. Replay the recorded weight-vector sequence in shuffled and reversed order to preserve its cumulative exposure and distribution while changing timing. With changing learning rates, also report Σ_t η_t w_k(t); matching coefficient sums does not match this learning-rate-weighted quantity. Neither measure guarantees equal gradient exposure under Adam or changing model parameters. These are proposed attribution controls, rather than a universal protocol established by the cited papers.

Use the same validation cadence, metric, checkpoint eligibility, and tie-breaking rule. Report both the fixed final checkpoint and the identically selected best-validation checkpoint: selection can otherwise obscure horizon matching. In the specified benchmark, retain seed 42 and the fixed epoch/batch limits. Improvement over the exposure-matched constant control supports a timing effect; improvement over shuffled/reversed schedules strengthens evidence for the proposed ordering. It does not establish that gradient magnitudes or optimization trajectories were matched.
